prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

The cycle lane is most positively rated on Physical Comfort and Ease of Use. Compared to the adjacent cycle path, the cycle lane has stronger lane markings which increases the Ease of Use for cyclists. Additionally, it runs on the road level next to the motor traffic and is usually better asphalted than cycle paths. This allows a more fluent cycling and increases the Physical Comfort. Interestingly, the cycle lane is rated slightly more negatively on Mental Comfort than on Interaction. A well marked cycle lane is often considered as a proper cycling facility that draws drivers’ attention to possible cyclists. However, although it separates from the motor traffic and, therefore, leads to less possible interactions, cyclists might perceive it as mentally uncomfortable because of a small width and a lack of feeling safe. Generally spoken, the less the cycling facility is separated the worse it is rated on the clusters. Surprisingly, the bicycle boulevard is evaluated similar to the least separated advisory lane, but with a much better rating in Mental Comfort. This indicates that a too weak separation can no longer induce a feeling of safety or Mental Comfort, and below this threshold of separation, cyclists might prefer bicycle boulevards which draw attention to cyclists as road users, but in principle have no separation at all. More concrete, cyclists may prefer no separation over a too weak one. Bicycle boulevards are also evaluated more positively than residential roads, although in Germany, bicycle boulevards are usually open for motorized traffic and the traffic regulations are, hence, the same as for residential roads. The only difference are traffic signs that highlight cyclists as road users who must not be endangered by motor vehicles, and that cyclists are allowed to cycle side by side (Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection, 2020). On the one hand, this may lead to a stronger self-confidence of the cyclists towards other road users. On the other hand, cyclists may associate a bicycle boulevard with even lower traffic volume, lower traffic speed, and more cooperative and careful interactions with other road users which increases their perception of Interaction, Environment, and Mental Comfort compared to the residential road. The shared footpath is evaluated neither good nor bad on all the clusters. The Mental and Physical Comfort are even lower than at bicycle boulevards and shared spaces. Cyclists may feel uncomfortable here as they cycle on a way which is mainly for walking, and cycling is only tolerated. Cyclists are, thus, in the position of the stronger road user that must be considerate towards the weaker and slower pedestrians. Also, cyclists need to watch out for people leaving buildings or properties and suddenly stepping onto the footpath. All this might be perceived as stressful and as hindering the cycling flow. No visible curb ramps, tactile paving, marked crossings, or dedicated pedestrian facilities can be identified in the scene, limiting evidence that the design is equally accessible and non-discriminatory for diverse users.
safety: The roadway is wide, straight, and well marked with clear centerlines and lane lines, which supports predictable vehicle movement and reduces immediate conflict risk for drivers.
Streetlights are installed continuously along both sides, which suggests basic nighttime visibility infrastructure even though daytime conditions are shown.

Very low visible traffic volume reduces short-term collision pressure, but the broad carriageway and long uninterrupted alignment may encourage higher driving speeds, which can reduce overall safety for all road users.
livability: The corridor is dominated by a broad asphalt roadway with little visible street-edge activity, shops, seating, or human presence, so it appears more like a movement corridor than a socially active place.
Landscaped planting beds and mature trees improve environmental quality and visual pleasantness, contributing somewhat to everyday livability.
No visible benches, bus stops, kiosks, or gathering spaces are present, limiting support for daily social use beyond passing through.
sustainability: The strong tree canopy and continuous roadside greenery provide shade, carbon uptake, and ecological value compared with a fully hardscaped corridor.
Landscaped strips along both sides likely increase permeable surface area relative to the road itself, which is favorable for stormwater absorption.

However, no visible bus stop, bike lane, or other clearly marked low-carbon transport facility is present, so sustainability benefits come mainly from greening rather than multimodal transport support.
aesthetics: The avenue has a strong visual rhythm created by evenly spaced trees and consistently designed streetlights on both sides.
Mature green vegetation and flowering groundcover along the edges create an attractive, well-maintained landscape character.
The roadway appears clean, uncluttered, and visually coherent, with long sightlines and minimal visual disorder.
comfort: Large roadside trees cast shade onto the edges of the street, which improves thermal comfort near the margins even though the central roadway remains exposed.
The pavement surface looks smooth and even, supporting physical comfort for wheeled movement such as driving or cycling if permitted.

The scene is spacious and uncrowded, which likely reduces psychological stress from congestion, but the very wide road and lack of visible pedestrian amenities may feel less comfortable for people outside vehicles.
walkability: No clearly visible sidewalk, crosswalk, refuge island, or pedestrian path can be confirmed in the image, which weakens basic walking support.
The street is very wide and designed primarily around multiple traffic lanes, making pedestrian crossing likely difficult where no marked crossing is visible.
Although trees and landscaped edges could make walking more pleasant if a path exists off-frame, the visible evidence does not show continuous pedestrian infrastructure needed for strong walkability.

prompt_c3:
As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

1. All scores must include one decimal place.
2. Each array in explanations must contain at least 3 reasons based on specific objects in the image (e.g., benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings).

The cycle lane is most positively rated on Physical Comfort and Ease of Use. Compared to the adjacent cycle path, the cycle lane has stronger lane markings which increases the Ease of Use for cyclists. Additionally, it runs on the road level next to the motor traffic and is usually better asphalted than cycle paths. This allows a more fluent cycling and increases the Physical Comfort. Interestingly, the cycle lane is rated slightly more negatively on Mental Comfort than on Interaction. A well marked cycle lane is often considered as a proper cycling facility that draws drivers’ attention to possible cyclists. However, although it separates from the motor traffic and, therefore, leads to less possible interactions, cyclists might perceive it as mentally uncomfortable because of a small width and a lack of feeling safe. Generally spoken, the less the cycling facility is separated the worse it is rated on the clusters. Surprisingly, the bicycle boulevard is evaluated similar to the least separated advisory lane, but with a much better rating in Mental Comfort. This indicates that a too weak separation can no longer induce a feeling of safety or Mental Comfort, and below this threshold of separation, cyclists might prefer bicycle boulevards which draw attention to cyclists as road users, but in principle have no separation at all. More concrete, cyclists may prefer no separation over a too weak one. Bicycle boulevards are also evaluated more positively than residential roads, although in Germany, bicycle boulevards are usually open for motorized traffic and the traffic regulations are, hence, the same as for residential roads. The only difference are traffic signs that highlight cyclists as road users who must not be endangered by motor vehicles, and that cyclists are allowed to cycle side by side (Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection, 2020). On the one hand, this may lead to a stronger self-confidence of the cyclists towards other road users. On the other hand, cyclists may associate a bicycle boulevard with even lower traffic volume, lower traffic speed, and more cooperative and careful interactions with other road users which increases their perception of Interaction, Environment, and Mental Comfort compared to the residential road. The shared footpath is evaluated neither good nor bad on all the clusters. The Mental and Physical Comfort are even lower than at bicycle boulevards and shared spaces. Cyclists may feel uncomfortable here as they cycle on a way which is mainly for walking, and cycling is only tolerated. Cyclists are, thus, in the position of the stronger road user that must be considerate towards the weaker and slower pedestrians. Also, cyclists need to watch out for people leaving buildings or properties and suddenly stepping onto the footpath. All this might be perceived as stressful and as hindering the cycling flow.
